dervis-irab:1-8.t:
* Vocabulary:
(مُنْفَكِّينَ) The infikāk of one thing from another is that it separates from it after having been joined to it, like a bone when it is dislocated from its joint. The meaning is that they cling to their religion, neither leaving it nor seeking to be released from it. Al-Azharī said: "It is not of the category of mā infakka and mā bariḥa [kāna's sisters]; rather it is of the category of the detachment of one thing from another, i.e., its separation from it."
(حُنَفاءَ) Inclining toward good. The lexicographers said: the origin of al-ḥanaf in the language is inclination, and usage specialised it to inclination toward good, while they called inclination toward evil ilḥād. In al-Qāmūs: "Al-ḥanaf, with vowels on the letters: straightness, and crookedness in the foot; or that one puts one of the big toes of the feet before the other; or that one walks on the back of the feet on the side of the little toe; or an inclination in the front of the foot. Ḥanifa (like fariḥa and karuma), so he is aḥnaf, and a man is ḥanfāʾ; and, like ḍaraba, he inclined. And Ṣakhr Abū Baḥr al-Aḥnaf ibn Qays was a great Follower; the Ḥanīfī swords are attributed to him because he was the first to order that they be made, though the analogical form would be Aḥnafī. Al-ḥanfāʾ: the bow, the razor, the mare of Ḥudhayfa ibn Badr, a watering place of Banū Muʿāwiya, a tree, the changeable slave-woman who is lazy at one time and active at another, the chameleon, the tortoise, and al-uṭūm [a sea fish]. Al-ḥanīf, like amīr: the one who is sound in his inclination to Islam and firm in it; everyone who performed the pilgrimage or was of the religion of Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him; the poor man; and the one who goes barefoot," up to where he says: "Abū Ḥanīfa is the kunya of twenty jurists, the most famous being the imām of the jurists, al-Nuʿmān." The wording of Ibn Khālawayh is good, and it is: "(حنفاء) is accusative as ḥāl, like ẓarīf and ẓurafāʾ. Al-ḥanīf in the language is the straight one. If it is said to you, 'Why was the crooked-footed man called aḥnaf?', say: they took a good omen from crookedness toward straightness, as the bitten one is called 'sound', the blind man 'Abū Baṣīr', the black man 'Abū l-Bayḍāʾ', and the perilous desert mafāza ['place of salvation']. This is the view of most grammarians. As for Ibn al-Aʿrābī, he claimed that mafāza is not an inversion, because the Arabs say fawwaza l-rajul when he died, and likewise jannaṣa. The poet said:
فمن للقوافي بعدها من يحوكها إذا ما ثوى كعب وفوّز جرول
(Who will weave the rhymes after them, once Kaʿb has settled [in the grave] and Jarwal has passed away?)
He means Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr and Jarwal, that is, al-Ḥuṭayʾa. Al-ḥanīf is six things: the straight; the crooked; the Muslim; the sincere; the circumcised; and the one who makes pilgrimage to the House of Allah; and whoever acts by the sunna of Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, is called ḥanīf."

* I'rab:
(لَمْ يَكُنِ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتابِ وَالْمُشْرِكِينَ مُنْفَكِّينَ حَتَّى تَأْتِيَهُمُ الْبَيِّنَةُ) (لم) is a particle of negation, inversion and jussive; (يكن) is a defective imperfect verb jussive by (لن) [Translator's note: the source writes "by lan"; the jussive particle here is (لم), as stated just before]; (الذين) is its noun and the clause (كفروا) is the ṣila; (من أهل الكتاب والمشركين) is attached to an omitted element serving as ḥāl; the more probable view is that (من) here is partitive, as al-Māturīdī determined; (منفكين) is the khabar of (يكن); (حتى) is a particle of limit and genitive; (تأتيهم) is an imperfect verb in the subjunctive by an implied (أن) after (حتى); the hāʾ is a direct object; and (البينة) is the fāʿil, meaning the clear proof. (رَسُولٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ يَتْلُوا صُحُفاً مُطَهَّرَةً) (رسول) is a badal from (البينة), a total substitute (badal kull min kull) by way of hyperbole, the Messenger being made the clear proof itself; (من الله) is an adjective of (رسول); the clause (يتلو) is a second adjective, or a ḥāl according to the rule; (صحفا) is a direct object; and (مطهرة) is an adjective of (صحفا). (فِيها كُتُبٌ قَيِّمَةٌ) The clause is a second adjective of (صحفا); (فيها) is a preposed khabar, (كتب) a postposed mubtadaʾ, and (قيمة) an adjective of (كتب), meaning upright, speaking truth and justice. (وَما تَفَرَّقَ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْكِتابَ إِلَّا مِنْ بَعْدِ ما جاءَتْهُمُ الْبَيِّنَةُ) The wāw is resumptive and (ما) is negative; (تفرق الذين) is verb and fāʿil; the clause (أوتوا) has no grammatical position because it is the ṣila of (الذين); the wāw in (أوتوا) is the nāʾib fāʿil and (الكتاب) is a second direct object; (إلا) is a particle of restriction; (من بعد) are two elements attached to (تفرق); (ما) is maṣdarī; (جاءتهم البينة) is a past verb, a direct object and a postposed fāʿil; and (ما) with what is in its scope is in the position of genitive through the annexation of (بعد) to it. It is a matter of the utmost astonishment that Ibn Khālawayh parsed (ما) as a relative, and there is no justification at all for this parsing; his amusing wording is: "(ما) means 'that which' (alladhī), and it is genitive by (بعد)." (وَما أُمِرُوا إِلَّا لِيَعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ مُخْلِصِينَ لَهُ الدِّينَ حُنَفاءَ وَيُقِيمُوا الصَّلاةَ وَيُؤْتُوا الزَّكاةَ وَذلِكَ دِينُ الْقَيِّمَةِ) The wāw is for ḥāl, and the clause is a ḥāl clause, introduced to show how ugly and repugnant was what they did, namely dividing after the clear proof came, which every person with a grain of intellect must proclaim. (ما) is negative; (أمروا) is a passive past verb and the wāw is the nāʾib fāʿil, and what it is attached to is omitted, i.e., "with what We commanded them of laws and rulings"; (إلا) is a particle of restriction; (ليعبدوا): the lām is the causal lām, (يعبدوا) is an imperfect verb in the subjunctive by an implied (أن) after the lām, and the wāw is the fāʿil. The preposition and its genitive noun are attached to (أمروا), in the position of accusative as mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose); its being put in the accusative directly is prevented only because of the difference of agent. Perhaps this view is better than what al-Jalāl chose, whose wording is: "(إلا ليعبدوا الله) means 'that they worship Him', the (أن) having been omitted and the lām added." Al-Karkhī made the clay wetter still [i.e., made things worse] by saying: "His words 'the lām was added': the first (view) is that it means the bāʾ, i.e., 'except by worshipping Allah'." This is a forced and strained reading that does not befit the style of the Great Qur'an. Perhaps this notion seeped into the two of them from the reading of Ibn Masʿūd, (وما أمروا إلا أن يعبدوا); on that reading their statement would be acceptable and fitting, with (أن) and what is within its scope an interpreted maṣdar accusative by removal of the preposition, namely the bāʾ, with the preposition and its genitive noun attached to (أمروا), i.e., "to worship". (مخلصين) is a ḥāl from the pronoun of (يعبدوا); (له) are two elements attached to (مخلصين); (الدين) is the direct object of (مخلصين) because it is an active participle; (حنفاء) is a second ḥāl as stated before, or a ḥāl from the preceding ḥāl, or from the pronoun latent in it, so it is a nested ḥāl. (ويقيموا الصلاة) is conjoined to (ليعبدوا الله); (ويؤتوا الزكاة) is conjoined also; the wāw is a conjunction or a ḥāl wāw. (ذلك) is a mubtadaʾ, the pointer referring to what was mentioned of worshipping Allah, establishing prayer and paying zakāt; (دين) is the khabar; and (القيمة) is muḍāf ilayhi. Al-Farrāʾ said: "He annexed the religion to al-qayyima, which is its adjective, because the two words differ; or it is a case of annexing a thing to itself; and the tāʾ marbūṭa [the hāʾ] entered for praise and hyperbole; and the sense of distance in the demonstrative is to indicate the loftiness of its rank and the remoteness of its station." The wording of Ibn Khālawayh is good, and it is: "If it is said to you, 'The religion is the qayyima, so why did He not say wa-dhālika l-dīn al-qayyima?', say: the Arabs annex a thing to its adjective, as in their saying ṣalāt al-ẓuhr and ḥabb al-ḥaṣīd. The poet said:
أتمدح فقعسا وتذمّ عبسا ... ألا لله أمك من هجين
ولو أقوت عليك ديار عبس ... عرفت الذلّ عرفان اليقين
(Do you praise Faqʿas and revile ʿAbs? By Allah, your mother is of mixed stock! / Had the dwellings of ʿAbs been left desolate for you, you would have known abasement with the knowledge of certainty.)
Here he annexed 'knowledge' to 'certainty' when he meant 'certain knowledge'. Others said: 'that is the religion of the upright community' and 'that is the religion of the upright ḥanīfiyya', so the muḍāf was omitted and the muḍāf ilayhi put in its place, as Allah the Mighty and Exalted said: (وَاسْأَلِ الْقَرْيَةَ الَّتِي كُنَّا فِيهَا), i.e., ask its people." (إِنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتابِ وَالْمُشْرِكِينَ فِي نارِ جَهَنَّمَ خالِدِينَ فِيها أُولئِكَ هُمْ شَرُّ الْبَرِيَّةِ) A resumptive statement, introduced to begin explaining the abode of the wretched and the reward of the blessed. (إن) and its noun, and the clause (كفروا) is a ṣila with no grammatical position; (من أهل الكتاب والمشركين) is a ḥāl; (في نار جهنم) is the khabar of (إن); (خالدين) is an implied (muqaddara) ḥāl from the pronoun latent in the khabar; (فيها) are two elements attached to (خالدين); (أولئك) is a mubtadaʾ; (هم) is a second mubtadaʾ or a pronoun of separation; (شر البرية) is the khabar of (هم) and the clause is the khabar of (إن) or the khabar of (أولئك). (البريئة) was read with hamza in both places. It was said that the hamza is the origin, from bara'a Allāhu l-khalq, i.e., He originated and invented it, so barī'a is of the pattern fa'īla in the sense of maf'ūl. It was also said that (البرية) without hamza is derived from al-barā, which is dust, because they were created from it. Al-Maʿarrī said:
ولرب أجساد جديرات البرى ... بالصون صارت في طلاء جدار
(Many a body that deserved to be turned to dust, though guarded, has become plaster on a wall.)
It was also said that al-bariyya is a lightened form of the hamzated word. The wording of Ibn Khālawayh: "(البرية) is genitive by annexation; the original is barī'a, but they dropped the hamza for lightness; it is from bara'a Allāhu l-khalq, and Allah is al-Bāri' al-Muṣawwir. Ibrāhīm ibn ʿArafa related to us, saying: Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā related to us, saying: Muḥammad ibn Kathīr related to us from Sufyān from al-Mukhtār ibn Fulful from Anas, who said: A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and his family and said to him: 'O best of creation!' He said: 'That is Ibrāhīm, the Friend of the Most Merciful.' He said it only out of humility, may Allah bless him and grant him peace." (إِنَّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحاتِ أُولئِكَ هُمْ خَيْرُ الْبَرِيَّةِ) The clause is exactly like the first in its parsing. Ibn Khālawayh has useful remarks on al-bariyya, which we transmit as follows: "(البرية) is genitive by annexation. Al-ʿUjayr said to Nāfiʿ ibn ʿAlqama:
يا نافعا يا أكرم البريّة ... والله لا أكذبك العشيّه
إنّا لقينا سنة قسيّه ... ثم مطرنا مطرة رويّه
فنبت البقل ولا رعيّه ... فانظر بنا القرابة العليّه
والعرب مما ولدت صفيّه
(O Nāfiʿ, O most generous of creation, by Allah I will not lie to you this evening. / We met a harsh year, then we were rained upon with a plentiful rain; / the herbage grew, but no one grazes it. So look on us with the exalted kinship; and the Arabs, of those they have begotten, [we are] the choice ones.)
And he ordered a thousand sheep for him. Others said: whoever dropped the hamza from al-bariyya took it from al-barā, which is dust." Ibn Mujāhid recited to us: "Your transgression, whoever goes to your people, [is] the dust"; and in the speech of the Arabs the hamza is dropped. The poet said:
امرر على جدث الحسين فقل لأعظمه الزكيّة
قبر تضمن طيّبا ... آباؤه خير البريّة
آباؤه أهل الخلا ... فة والرياسة والعطية
(Pass by the grave of al-Ḥusayn and speak to his pure bones: a grave that holds a good man, whose fathers were the best of creation, / his fathers, the people of the caliphate, leadership and bounty.)
This is what Ibn Khālawayh cited, and in it there is a difficulty that must be pointed out, namely al-ʿUjayr's saying to Nāfiʿ ibn ʿAlqama (يا نافعا): he put the one addressed in the accusative, though it is a single proper name, and gave it tanwīn, whereas it should be indeclinable on ḍamma, and we found nothing to justify it. The grammarians have stated that when the one addressed is a single proper name described by "ibn" with no separation between them and the "ibn" is annexed to a proper name, two forms are permissible for the one addressed: ḍamma for indeclinability, and the accusative, as in yā ʿAmru bna Hindin and yā ʿAmra bna Hindin, the fatḥa being preferable. As for the ḍamma, it follows the rule because it is a single proper name; as for the accusative, it is on the consideration that the word "ibn" is redundant, so ʿAmr is muḍāf and Hind is muḍāf ilayhi, and the "son" of a person is annexed to him by reason of the connection between them. Description by "ibna" is like description by "ibn", as in yā Hindu bnata Khālid and yā Hinda bnata Khālid; but description by "bint" does not change the indeclinability of the single proper name, and with it only ḍamma is permissible, as in yā Hindu bnata Khālid. In any case, al-ʿUjayr's verse does not belong to this category, and it does not help to say that it is described by His words "most generous of creation" on the assumption of a redundant yā, because the description is not the word "ibn" or "ibna". Suppose he gave it tanwīn out of poetic necessity: why did he not keep it with ḍamma, like the saying of al-Aḥwaṣ:
سلام الله يا مطر عليها ... وليس عليك يا مطر السلام
(Allah's peace be upon her, O Maṭar, but upon you, O Maṭar, be no peace.)
The grammarians paid attention to this verse and called its tanwīn "tanwīn of necessity"; it is not so [convincing]; refer, if you wish, to their books. (جَزاؤُهُمْ عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ جَنَّاتُ عَدْنٍ تَجْرِي مِنْ تَحْتِهَا الْأَنْهارُ خالِدِينَ فِيها أَبَداً رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا عَنْهُ ذلِكَ لِمَنْ خَشِيَ رَبَّهُ) (جزاؤهم) is a mubtadaʾ; (عند ربهم) is an adverb attached to an omitted element serving as ḥāl from the pronoun in (جزاؤهم); (جنات عدن) is the khabar; the clause (تجري من تحتها الأنهار) is an adjective of (جنات); (خالدين) is a ḥāl from an omitted governor, whose implied form is "their entering it"; it cannot be a ḥāl from the pronoun in (جزاؤهم), lest it entail separation between the maṣdar and its dependent by an alien element; (فيها) are two elements attached to (خالدين); (أبدا) is an adverb of time for the totality of meaning, accusative by (خالدين) also. The clause (رضي الله عنهم ورضوا عنه) may be a supplication with no grammatical position, or it may be a second khabar. (ذلك) is a mubtadaʾ and (لمن) is its khabar, and the clause (خشي ربه) is a ṣila, also with no grammatical position.

* Benefits:
It may be useful to point out here the meaning of the servant's being pleased with Allah, which al-Rāghib summarised, saying: "The servant's pleasure with Allah is that he not dislike what His decree brings about, and Allah's pleasure with the servant is that He sees him obeying His command and refraining from His prohibition." As for al-Junayd, he said: "Pleasure (riḍā) is in proportion to the strength of knowledge and firmness in gnosis. Pleasure is a state that accompanies the servant in this world and the next, and its place is not the place of fear, hope, patience, apprehension and the other states that leave the servant in the Hereafter; rather the servant enjoys pleasure in Paradise and asks Allah, the Exalted, until He says to them: 'By My pleasure I settle you in My abode', i.e., by My pleasure with you." Muḥammad ibn al-Faḍl said: "Rest and comfort are in pleasure and certainty; and pleasure is the greatest door of Allah and the resting place of the worshippers."
